The Pied kingfisher (Ceryle rudis) exhibits a remarkable combination of life-history traits that reflect its specialization for piscivorous foraging along freshwater waterways. Hatchlings emerge from eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] after a developmental period of 15 days [ab = 15 days], an interval that aligns closely with the incubation durations documented among other members of the Alcedinidae. Upon hatching, these altricial nestlings possess an average body mass of just 8.1 grams [Ww0 = 8.1 grams], representing an extremely modest initial investment that is typical of species that produce multiple broods within a single breeding season. This low neonatal mass imposes a substantial parental burden, as the nestlings require near-constant brooding and provisioning during their initial weeks of life. The rapid growth trajectory that follows, fueled by a diet of small fish delivered by both parents, quickly transforms these diminutive chicks into fully formed juveniles capable of independent foraging within a relatively compressed developmental window.

Under the elevated thermal regime of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], which characterizes the metabolic conditions during the active period of this species, the developmental milestones unfold in a predictable sequence. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest cavity, occurs 25 days after hatching [tx = 25 days after hatching], a relatively abbreviated nestling period that reflects the energetic demands of an adult body size that must be approached rapidly at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. Following this transition to independent locomotion, the young birds enter a prolonged juvenile phase during which they must refine their hunting skills and accumulate sufficient lipid reserves to support the energetic costs of eventual reproduction. The age at which these individuals attain sexual maturity, indicated by the onset of gametogenesis and full gonadal development, is estimated at 75 days after hatching [tp = 75 days after hatching], a value that situates Ceryle rudis among the faster-maturing members of its family at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C].

Significant sexual size dimorphism is evident in the ultimate body masses attained by adult Pied kingfishers. Females reach a maximum recorded body mass of 86.4 grams [Wwi = 86.4 grams], whereas males are consistently smaller, achieving a mature weight of 82.4 grams [Wwi = 82.4 grams]. This difference of approximately 4 grams, though modest in absolute terms, is statistically robust across multiple populations and likely reflects differential selective pressures on the sexes, with the slightly larger female size facilitating the energetic demands of egg production and clutch incubation. The timing of first reproduction, representing the age at which a bird completes its first successful nesting attempt, occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] when individuals are maintained under typical thermal conditions of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This interval of approximately one full year between hatching and the initiation of breeding is relatively conservative for a species of this body size, potentially constrained by the need to acquire territory and establish a stable pair bond.

The maximum reproductive rate of Ceryle rudis is mediated through two complementary components that together define the species' annual output. Females typically lay 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 5 eggs per clutch], a clutch size that represents an energetic compromise between the demands of producing large, yolk-rich eggs and the capacity of the parents to provision the resulting brood. Across the breeding season, these birds exhibit a frequency of approximately 1.5 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 clutches per year], a value that reflects the extended breeding opportunities afforded by a tropical or subtropical climate with prolonged periods of prey availability. The combination of these parameters, which together yield an annual production rate of roughly 7.5 offspring per breeding adult, underscores the Pied kingfisher's status as a moderately fecund species within the kingfisher lineage. This reproductive strategy appears well adapted to environments where nest predation rates are moderate and where the availability of suitable nesting banks is not a primary limiting factor.

Longevity records for the Pied kingfisher, compiled from both field studies of banded populations and captive observations, indicate a maximum lifespan of 5 years [am = 5 years] when birds are maintained under the thermal conditions typical of their active metabolic phase at 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This relatively short maximum lifespan, compared to what might be predicted for a bird of its body mass, likely reflects the cumulative physiological costs associated with a life history characterized by high annual reproductive effort and a specialized, energetically demanding foraging mode. The sustained hover-hunting technique employed by this species, which requires repeated bouts of rapid wingbeats and precise aerial positioning, imposes substantial oxidative stress and metabolic wear that may accelerate the aging process. Furthermore, the high rates of predation on nesting adults by raptors and terrestrial predators, combined with the risks of accidental drowning during plunge-diving, contribute to an elevated extrinsic mortality rate that constrains the evolution of a longer lifespan.
